title: Microlasers Allow Force Measurements at Microscopic Scale
content: Mechanical forces play major roles in almost all aspects of biology. Mechanical force generation guides the development of early embryos as cells divide and reorganize to form an adult organism. The migration of immune cells into tissues to fight infections requires modulations of various forces. Muscular contraction requires the generation and dissipation of forces along multiple axes. Rapid cell division of cancer cells in confined spaces applies force on surrounding cells. Cells are constantly sensing, responding to, and generating mechanical forces. Because of the importance of measuring forces within cells and tissues, over the years many sophisticated methods have been developed to measure the strength of the various forces that modulate biological processes. These methods include measuring the displacement of a substrate (traction force microscopy) [1,2], atomic force microscopy (AFM) [3], optical and magnetic tweezers [4,5], and the injection of small compressible materials [6]. Most of these techniques rely on high-resolution microscopy and are difficult or impossible to implement in dense material.
